> Create an activity called Heater.

Actually, try it this way:

Create a custom device in Harmony called Heater.  Teach that custom device the IR codes from your heater's remote.  Then, assign your custom Heater device to whichever buttons in whichever activities you want - or even all activities if that's what you want.  Or, since you mentioned not needing remote buttons, this will group all of the functions in the custom device in the Harmony app.

I did this with my Philips Hue lights because I didn't like how Harmony works with Hue.  I was already using the Hue API with a Flirc IR receiver to control my lights with a remote.  So, I created a custom device in Harmony for Flirc, and I taught Harmony the IR codes I wanted to use.  Then, I assigned that custom Flirc device to all of my Harmony activities & I set my Harmony remote buttons up the way I wanted to control my lights.

It sounds complicated, but it was actually pretty easy.

TIP!  Think about how you want to name the IR codes from your remote when you teach them to Harmony.  Each one will get a name, and Harmony won't let you edit the names for the IR codes, so make sure you name them in a way that makes sense.  For example, I named mine Hue Bright, Hue Ambiance, Hue TV, Hue Mood Light, etc, that way all of my custom Hue IR codes were grouped together.

Here's an example:

Like I said, I created a custom device called a universal IR receiver. I added my receiver device to every activity, but didn't give it a power button (it doesn't have one, obviously, since it's not an actual device in the normal sense). So, when I start an activity, my remote buttons are set up and ready to go, but lights didn't turn on since I didn't assign any of them to turn on when I start that activity.

> I am annoyed that a remote manufacturer assumes all uses of one’s AV equipment is done in the dark and involves sitting and viewing a TV screen.

Yeah, there are a lot of screwy things about that remote system. You can usually find other ways to accomplish what you want though. For example, you can assign your TV to more than one activity, and you can assign whatever controls your music to your Watch TV activity too. It's all flexible - this also makes it complicated to set up since you have to give it more thought than you would with a simple remote, but it's worth it in the end.

The trick is to think about activities instead of devices.

Here's how I do it - and I'll preface this by saying I had most of this set up long before I bought a Harmony last year.

1. Scripts on my Mac to control the Hue API.

2. Hotkeys on my Mac to trigger the scripts.

3. A Flirc usb IR receiver for my Mac to trigger the hotkeys.

4. A custom device on Harmony for remote buttons to trigger Flirc for the hotkeys.

I know that sounds complicated, but it's actually not. I set it up years ago to repurpose an Apple remote to control my Hue. Last year, I added Harmony into the mix and it's worked perfectly.

First, I wrote Applescripts for my Mac to trigger all sorts of things using the Hue API (scenes, dimming, etc. I had a system for dimming before Hue added bri_inc into the API). Next, I created hotkeys to trigger my Hue Applescripts (BetterTouchTool is awesome for this, but you can also do it using Mac keyboard prefs. Surely Windows has a way to do this too. On a Raspberry Pi, use the TriggerHappy daemon).

I bought a Flirc usb IR receiver back in... 2013? Flirc is awesome. Flirc translates remote IR commands into hotkeys you set up. So... I taught Flirc which remote buttons trigger which Hue Applescripts.

You could do the same thing with a PC or even a Raspberry Pi. In fact, a Raspberry Pi would be perfect.

Breathe in.  Short pause.  Breathe out.  99.

Breathe in.  Short pause.  Breathe out.  97.    
Breathe in.  Short pause.  Breathe out.  96.

If you're having an especially hard time falling asleep, double up on the counting.  Breathe in.  Pause to count.  Breathe out.  Pause to count.  Again, the pause should only be short.  Your goal is to build up a nice steady rhythm without thinking about it.

Writing scripts to control your stuff can be a giant pain in the butt, but it's time well spent because it's slick in use.

I use this setup mostly for triggering all kinds of stuff, but especially Philips Hue scenes.  I use the red/green/yellow/blue buttons on my Harmony remote to trigger Hue lights & scenes.  Each button is assigned to a scene, and pressing it a second time triggers an alt version of the scene (and logs it to a Current_Hue_Scene text file I use to keep track).

For example, pressing the Green button triggers my Hue "Ambiance" scene unless the Current_Hue_Scene file is currently set to "Ambiance" in which case the green button triggers "Mood_Light" instead.

I'm sure there are other ways to accomplish something similar, but this is how I do it.

I am a huuuuuuuuuuuuge fan of using a Raspberry Pi and a Flirc IR receiver with Harmony.  Anything I can script, I can control at the press of a button with Harmony.
